This page corresponds to U.S. O*NET/SOC 19-3092.00, “Geographers” (the fixed Chinese index title translates as “Geographers”; common recruitment and industry titles include geographer, geographic information coordinator, Earth observation scientist and geographic information physical scientist). The official scope is to study the nature and use of areas of the Earth's surface, relating and interpreting interactions between physical and cultural phenomena; study an area's physical aspects (landforms, climate, soils, plants and animals) and the spatial effects of human activities within particular areas (social characteristics, economic activities and political organization); and study interdependencies between areas from local to global scales. O*NET's core tasks include creating and modifying maps, charts and diagrams using geographic information software and related equipment and cartographic principles such as coordinate systems, latitude and longitude, elevation, terrain and scale (importance 84); collecting and compiling geographic data from censuses, field observations, satellite imagery, aerial photographs and existing maps (79); teaching geography (79); writing and presenting research reports (78); providing geographic information system support to the private and public sectors (73); studying the economic, political and cultural characteristics of populations in particular areas (71); analyzing the geographic distribution of physical and cultural phenomena at local, regional, continental or global scales (71); developing, operating and maintaining geographic information computer systems, including hardware, software, plotters, digitizers, printers and cameras (70); locating and obtaining existing geographic information databases (70); collecting data on an area's physical characteristics, including geological formations, climate and vegetation, using surveying or meteorological equipment (67); conducting fieldwork at outdoor sites (65); and consulting on resource development and management, business location, market-area analysis, environmental hazards, regional cultural history, and urban and social planning (55). Work is characterized by email (90% daily), work in controlled indoor environments (75% daily), substantial freedom to determine tasks, priorities and goals (55% report a lot of freedom), freedom to make decisions (50% report a lot of freedom), and typical workweeks exceeding 40 hours (55%). ONet's 2024 industry distribution shows government 79% and education 12%; the remaining 9% is only an arithmetic remainder. OOH's 2025 figures use another classification: federal government 64% (excluding postal services), education 13%, state government 10% (excluding education and hospitals), and professional, scientific and technical services 6%. Do not mix the two periods and classifications.

Paper learning observation | Complete the full G1 exercise (M1–M6) in the path section; this page provides all data, formulas, reference results and handover deadlines. Use pen and paper to deliver calculation, coverage-discrepancy and handover tables in 60 minutes. Recalculate population densities 500/800, the whole-area value 600, and service points per thousand residents 6/5. Do not fabricate missing information about coordinates, mixed boundaries, equity or requests for real household data. No equipment or expert is required; do not conduct real research or send materials externally. Record only this learning performance.

Signs of fit | Work-activity importance for U.S. O*NET 19-3092.00 shows that analyzing data or information (90), working with computers (89), processing information (88), getting information (86), updating and using relevant knowledge (81), interpreting the meaning of information for others (80), documenting and recording information (78), communicating with supervisors, peers or subordinates (75), and thinking creatively (75) are the occupation's most important activities. Work context shows email 90% daily, controlled indoor environments 75% daily, determining tasks, priorities and goals 55% reporting a lot of freedom, freedom to make decisions 50% reporting a lot of freedom, typical workweeks 55% reporting more than 40 hours, telephone conversations 75% reporting weekly or more often but not daily, prolonged sitting 60% reporting more than half the time, importance of being exact or highly accurate 30% reporting extremely important and 35% very important, and working in or contributing to a team 50% reporting very important. If you are willing to work with spatial data, maps and analysis over the long term, examine literature as well as data and definitions for a research or application question, and clearly document methods, limitations and uncertainty, this occupation's daily requirements are closer to your working style.

Reasons for caution | O*NET also shows (19-3092.00): prolonged sitting 60% reporting more than half the time; typical workweeks 55% reporting more than 40 hours; importance of being exact or highly accurate 30% reporting extremely important and 35% very important; time pressure 45% reporting weekly or more often but not daily; competition 50% reporting moderate competition; public speaking 45% reporting yearly or more often but not monthly; dealing with external customers or the public 45% reporting important; and coordinating or leading others 55% reporting important. U.S. employment in this occupation is very small (approximately 1,500 people in 2025), with a projected −2.1% in 2025–2035 (a slight decline). Total jobs and new opportunities are limited, and academic and government roles often depend on project cycles and funding. This occupation works with spatial data and research or application conclusions. A single error in data definitions, boundaries or projections, a mismatch between statistical coverage and conclusions, or inappropriate external provision of controlled or personal information data can make conclusions unusable and cause consequences. Processing citizens' personal information and controlled geographic information is also subject to applicable laws and competent authority requirements. If you struggle to work with data, literature and definitional details over the long term, accept uncertainty from funding and project cycles, or take responsibility for reliable conclusions and data compliance, treat these as practical costs requiring careful consideration.

Responsibility observation | In G1, record how you calculate, identify boundaries from different years, list unknown coordinate information and limitations, retain original values and actual times, and draft a handover awaiting confirmation. The three tables describe only this learning exercise, not long-term fit, formal research or authorization. Occupational judgments also require sustained courses, projects and actual role conditions.

Work can be divided into: (one) data collection and compilation—collecting and compiling geographic data from censuses, field observations, satellite imagery, aerial photographs and existing maps, locating and obtaining existing geographic information databases, and recording sources, definitions and accuracy; (two) spatial analysis and research—analyzing the geographic distribution of physical and cultural phenomena at local, regional, continental or global scales and studying the economic, political and cultural characteristics of populations in particular areas; (three) cartography and visualization—creating and modifying maps, charts and diagrams using geographic information software, related equipment and cartographic principles such as coordinate systems, latitude and longitude, elevation, terrain and scale; (four) systems and databases—developing, operating and maintaining geographic information computer systems, including hardware, software, plotters, digitizers, printers and cameras, with data ingestion, metadata and version management; (five) deliverables and teaching—writing and presenting research reports, undertaking teaching and training as required by the role, and providing geographic information system support to the private and public sectors; and (six) consulting and applications—consulting on resource development and management, business location, market-area analysis, environmental hazards, regional cultural history, and urban and social planning. The work cycle connects research or application questions and data-definition confirmation, data collection and compilation, coordinate and quality control, spatial analysis and mapping, explanations of results, limitations and uncertainty, and review, publication or delivery, and archiving. Do not make unauthorized judgments or promises on matters beyond your authority, including policy, legal or ethical conclusions and provision of controlled data. Pause and escalate or hand over conflicts in data definitions, boundary or projection errors, potentially misleading results or suspected data leaks. Better suited to people interested in methodological design, statistical inference and uncertainty analysis; this occupation emphasizes spatial phenomena, data compilation and explanations of geographic mechanisms.

Outputs comprise statistical designs, inference conclusions and uncertainty explanations.

Better suited to people interested in machine learning, data products and engineering implementation; this occupation emphasizes data compilation, analysis and explanation for spatial questions.

Core work and outputs: clean and integrate data, engineer features, model and validate, evaluate model performance, deploy and monitor data products, and explain results to business stakeholders. Outputs comprise models, assessments and data product reports.

What personality is better suited to being a geographer? This occupation places more weight on rigor with data, methods and definitions, sustained curiosity about regional and spatial phenomena, ability to clearly explain complex conclusions, and willingness to take responsibility for data compliance and reliable conclusions than on a personality type. O*NET's interest code is IR (Investigative–Realistic), and work styles emphasize innovation, intellectual curiosity, attention to detail and dependability, providing starting points for exploration.

Are introverts suited to this occupation? Yes. It involves extensive independent data processing, literature work and writing, alongside communication with data providers, project teams and readers (email 90% daily; telephone 75% weekly or more often but not daily; working in or contributing to a team 50% very important).

Can extraverts do it well? Communication is a task requirement; introversion or extraversion labels alone cannot establish performance. Observe how you explain data and limitations, confirm understanding and handle disagreements.

Which MBTI type is best for this occupation? No type has been proven best. MBTI is not an occupational qualification or ability assessment tool; occupational adaptation mainly depends on awareness of data and methods, adherence to methods, and software, writing and compliance capabilities.

Which Holland interest types are better suited to this occupation? O*NET's interest code is IR: Investigative (analyzing and investigating spatial, physical and cultural phenomena and developing and applying methods) and Realistic (working with practical objects such as maps, geographic information, equipment and fieldwork). Use it to explore task preferences, not predict performance.

This page has obtained no specific validity evidence for personality or interest scores predicting geographers' performance, so they cannot support individual predictions. One G1 exercise records only this learning experience; keep observing through later courses and projects.

Can I do this occupation if I am weak at mathematics? It requires quantitative abilities in statistics, spatial analysis and data processing, with daily data analysis, charts and calculations involving definitions. Quantitative foundations can be improved through training, but a complete inability to adapt to data and quantitative work is a significant limitation.

This occupation requires communication, collaboration and handling of disagreement. Observe how you check according to methods, explain limitations and hand over matters. This page sets no emotional intelligence threshold or predictions of emotional assessment effects.

Can the Enneagram determine whether I am suited to it? No. The Enneagram is a self-exploration tool, not a conclusion about occupational ability or fit. Assess fit by whether you can compile and analyze data and publish deliverables under data, method and definitional requirements.

Use this page's three G1 paper drafts to observe calculation, definitional checking and handover performance in this exercise. Compare your work with reference results and record errors and training needs, then keep observing through sustained courses and projects. Do not treat one task as proof of long-term fit or authorization.

paragraphs: Boundary | The following are failure scenarios inferred from tasks and editorial control suggestions; no frequency or severity ranking has been established. Check processing requirements against actual data classification, project, duties, jurisdiction and authorization. Do not equate all geographic research with licensed surveying and mapping or universally require administrative approval for all sharing or sensitive topics.

Risk examples include inconsistent definitions, uncontrolled original records or versions, unauthorized data provision, issuing deliverables beyond authority and interruptions to collaboration. This is not a ranking of incidence or consequences. First check sources, years, boundaries and methods and record reviews. Data classification and activity scope determine applicable rules; pause the affected stage and obtain supporting evidence for anomalies according to actual procedures.

Evidence scope | This page draws on O*NET 19-3092.00 tasks and work context (creating and modifying maps, charts and diagrams 84; collecting and compiling geographic data 79; teaching geography 79; writing and presenting research reports 78; providing geographic information system support to the private and public sectors 73; studying regional population characteristics 71; analyzing the geographic distribution of physical and cultural phenomena 71; maintaining geographic information computer systems 70; locating and obtaining existing geographic information databases 70; analyzing data or information 90; working with computers 89; processing information 88; getting information 86; updating and using relevant knowledge 81; interpreting the meaning of information for others 80; email 90% daily; controlled indoor environments 75% daily; prolonged sitting 60% more than half the time; importance of being exact or highly accurate 30% extremely important and 35% very important; time pressure 45% weekly or more often but not daily; competition 50% moderate). Data, deliverable and ethics management requirements refer to data protection, surveying and mapping deliverable, statistical and ethics management rules. Wage and employment figures use exact occupational coverage, but the base is small and a slight decline is projected; they serve only as background, not for risk assessment.
You, data and project roles; clients, the public and the research community

Misjudging data years, administrative boundaries, coordinate systems, projections or statistical coverage, combining or comparing data with incomparable definitions, or lacking traceable metadata and sources may cause systematically incorrect analysis conclusions and affect research, decisions and public understanding.

Before the task, check data sources, years, boundaries, coordinates and statistical coverage and record the basis. Check analysis and mapping according to methods and reproducibility requirements, retaining scripts and intermediate results. Immediately pause, review and redo work when definitions conflict, boundaries or projections are wrong, or results are abnormal.

Scenario | Regional boundaries and statistical data supplied for a project have inconsistent definitions. The schedule is tight, and the client wants maps and conclusions produced from existing data first and checked later.
You, data and quality roles; organizations, research or projects, and competent authorities

False, missing or fabricated original data, processing scripts, methods or metadata; backdated or untraceable rewrites; or inconsistent versions of results, drawings and databases affect reproducibility, quality, ethics and data-management checks, and credibility of deliverables.

Accurately record sources, scripts, parameters, original values and versions. Correct or supplement errors or omissions according to procedures, retaining original records, reasons, actual times and responsible persons. Do not fabricate observations, backdate, selectively delete data or fill gaps with unverified content.

Scenario | At handover, the previous shift's analysis scripts lack parameter and data-version records, and the result drawings and database have inconsistent versions. You are advised to fill the gaps using a template.
You, data, compliance and ethics roles; organizations, clients and data subjects

Failure to manage citizens' personal information or controlled or state-secret geographic information according to minimum necessity, approval, confidentiality and ethics requirements, or unauthorized external publication, provision or cross-border transfer, may violate data protection, surveying and mapping deliverable and ethics requirements and cause legal and reputational consequences.

Check whether materials contain identifiable personal information, controlled data or state secrets, and their actual purpose, recipient and authorization. Process them under applicable grounds, necessary scope and retention periods. External provision of state-secret deliverables requires approval under the rules; ordinary sharing does not universally require administrative approval. Report suspected unauthorized conduct according to procedures and retain facts.
Scenario | A stakeholder requests that data containing personal information or controlled geographic information be sent in an uncontrolled group chat for quick coordination.
You, legal, ethics and statistics roles; organizations, clients and professional practice

Publishing conclusions or making policy, legal or ethical conclusions beyond authorization, or issuing deliverables in place of statistical or qualified surveying and mapping roles, may cause legal, practice and reputational risks.

Publish deliverables within authorization and project scope. Hand over policy, legal, ethical, statistical or surveying and mapping qualification conclusions to the appropriate roles or organizations. When asked to exceed authorization, first explain the boundary and hand over according to procedures.
Scenario | During a staff shortage, you are asked to issue conclusions or deliverables with policy, legal or qualification effect beyond your organization's or your own authorization.
You, team and data-platform roles; project progress and deliverable continuity

When one person handles critical data, analysis or platform access, departure, interrupted funding, data-source changes or expired accounts may interrupt research or applications, delaying projects and affecting quality and continuity of deliverables.

Establish backup and handover rules for data, analysis scripts, platform access and personnel. Keep critical methods, parameters and result versions reproducible and recorded. Report staffing, access or funding shortages according to procedures and adjust priorities; do not publish conclusions with unresolved hazards.

Scenario | The only colleague familiar with particular data definitions and processing workflows is on leave. The project requires that colleague to guide untrained staff by telephone to process and publish results temporarily.
You, outsourcing providers and data service providers; projects, deliverables and data security

Unclear delivery and acceptance arrangements for outsourced data collection, analysis or platform services, or unclear data and deliverable ownership or fee-change rules, may cause rework, fee disputes and unclear quality and data-security responsibilities.

For outsourcing and technical cooperation, clearly define and record scope, standards, acceptance, data and deliverable ownership, and fee-change rules. Review and accept delivered results. Pause, review and report disputes about delivery, acceptance or ownership.

Scenario | After completing analysis, an outsourcing provider requests payment without submitting original data, scripts or checking records. On site, you are asked to sign off first, with data and review to follow later.

subject.summary: Geographers correspond to U.S. O*NET/SOC 19-3092.00, “Geographers”: they study the nature and use of areas of the Earth's surface, relating and interpreting interactions between physical and cultural phenomena. They study an area's physical aspects (landforms, climate, soils, plants and animals), the spatial effects of human activities within particular areas (social characteristics, economic activities and political organization), and interdependencies between areas from local to global scales. Core work includes collecting and compiling geographic data from censuses, field observations, satellite imagery, aerial photographs and existing maps; analyzing the geographic distribution of physical and cultural phenomena at multiple scales; studying the economic, political and cultural characteristics of populations in particular areas; creating and modifying maps, charts and diagrams using geographic information software and cartographic principles; developing, operating and maintaining geographic information computer systems and locating and obtaining existing geographic information databases; writing and presenting research reports and providing geographic information system support to the private and public sectors; and consulting on resource development and management, business location, market-area analysis, environmental hazards, and urban and social planning. Original official scope: Study the nature and use of areas of the Earth's surface, relating and interpreting interactions of physical and cultural phenomena. Wage and employment coverage: wages use O*NET's 2025 OEWS figures for this exact occupation; 2025–2035 employment projections come directly from BLS Table 1.2 (O*NET currently still displays the older period).
